::: {.lead}
The producer of *Byte Bay* wants a one-page comparison of Android and iOS
for *Pocket Quest*, with a recommendation. Rami starts to search the
Internet and finds hundreds of pages: official help pages, market reports,
forums, shops and old blogs. Some say the opposite of others. In lecture 15
you compared the two platforms. In this seminar you do it **yourself**,
like a professional: you choose the criteria, you find **reliable sources**
and write their dates, you build a comparison table, and you write a short
recommendation. Every section ends with a task, and at the end you have
your own one-page comparison.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary comparison-criteria reliable-source market-share developer-account app-review fragmentation >}}

## 16.1 Criteria and reliable sources

A comparison starts with the questions it must answer: the **criteria**.
Then each answer needs a source that you can trust (@fig-crit).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 16.1 — Criteria and reliable sources"}
**Comparison criteria** are the points you compare, chosen for the
decision (for a game launch: reach, costs, tools, testing, review,
updates). A **reliable source** has a known author or organisation, a
**date**, and shows its data. The best source for a fact about a platform
is its **maker's official page**.
:::

![Six criteria for Pocket Quest, and good and weak sources.](images/criteria-sources.png){#fig-crit width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 16.1 — Three sources for one fact"}
Rami needs the price of Apple's developer account.

1. Apple's developer page, updated this year: 99 USD per year. **Use it.**
2. A blog from 2019: "about 100 dollars". Old and rounded: do not use it.
3. A forum post: "I think it is free now". No author, no date: do not use
   it.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Taking the first search result. The first result is often an
advertisement or an old page. Look for the maker's page or a dated report.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/source-check.html" poster="sims/source-check.png" title="Source Check: can you trust this source?" height="560" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Judge five sources"}
1. In **Source Check**, judge all five sources.
2. Write the criteria of your own comparison: at least five, for Pocket
   Quest.

*Your result:* your score in Source Check and your list of criteria.
:::

## 16.2 The comparison table

A comparison table puts the two platforms side by side, one criterion per
line, with the source and its date (@fig-table).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 16.2 — A comparison table"}
A good comparison table has: one **row** per criterion; one **column** per
platform; a **source** column with the name and the **date** of each
source; short, exact cells (numbers with units). Facts that change (shares,
fees) always get a date.
:::

![A comparison table with a source for every line.](images/comparison-table.png){#fig-table width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 16.2 — Rami's first lines"}
1. Reach: Android about 70 %, iOS about 30 %; source: a market report,
   with the month and the year.
2. Account: 25 USD once, 99 USD per year; source: the help pages of Google
   Play and Apple, read on the day of the comparison.
3. Build: any PC, a Mac with Xcode; source: the developer pages of Android
   and Apple.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Cells like "better", "cheaper", "good". They are opinions. Write the fact
("25 USD once") and keep the opinion for the recommendation.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Build your table"}
1. In Word or Excel, make a table with the columns criterion, Android,
   iOS, source (date).
2. Fill at least five rows, each with a reliable source and its date.

*Your result:* a comparison table with five rows or more.
:::

## 16.3 A recommendation

The producer does not want only facts, but also advice. A
recommendation joins the facts of the table with the situation of the
studio (@fig-rec).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 16.3 — A recommendation"}
A good recommendation says **what** to do, **why** (two or three facts
from the table), and **what would change it**. It fits the situation of
the studio: its computers, its budget and its players.
:::

![From the table to a recommendation.](images/recommendation.png){#fig-rec width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 16.3 — Rami's advice"}
"Launch Pocket Quest on Android first. Byte Bay has only Windows PCs, and
an iOS build needs a Mac. Most of our players have budget Android phones,
and the Google Play account costs 25 USD once. When the studio has a Mac,
add iOS: few test devices, and players who often spend more."
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
A recommendation without reasons ("Android is the best"), or with a reason
that is not in the table. Every "because" needs a fact with a source.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Write your advice"}
1. Write a recommendation of three to five sentences for Pocket Quest.
2. Underline the facts from your table in it.

*Your result:* a short recommendation with underlined facts.
:::

## Case study: Fact or Myth?

Rami's first table has lines from the Internet: an iOS build needs a Mac
with Xcode; Android games are always slower than iPhone games; about 7 in
10 phones in the world run Android; the Google Play account costs 25 USD
once; iPhones cannot get viruses; and a game for Android must be tested on
several models. He must decide for each line: a fact with an official
source, a fact that changes and needs a dated report, or a myth. The Game
challenge of the interactive lesson uses these lines. In the mini-game
below you sort them.

## Further reading

Apple Developer, "Choosing a membership"; Google Play Console Help,
"Register for a Google Play Developer account"; Android Developers, "Test
your app". Check the date shown on each page.

## Exercises

1. What are comparison criteria? Give three for a game launch.
2. Name three signs of a reliable source.
3. Which source is best for the fee of a developer account?
4. Why does a market share need a date?
5. What is wrong with a cell that says "better"?
6. Which columns does a comparison table need?
7. Is "Android games are always slower" a fact? Why?
8. What three parts does a good recommendation have?
9. Rami's studio buys a Mac. Which part of his recommendation changes?
10. A blog from 2019 gives a price. What do you do?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. The points you compare; for example reach, account costs, test phones.
2. A known author or organisation, a date, and its data.
3. The official page of the store (Google Play Console Help, Apple
   Developer).
4. Shares change from month to month.
5. It is an opinion, not a fact.
6. Criterion, Android, iOS, source (date).
7. No: it depends on the phone; "always" is a warning sign.
8. What to do, why (facts), and what would change it.
9. The iOS part: an iOS build is now possible.
10. Find the price on the official page today.
:::
